segments.say: In nineteen ninety six, a philosophy professor at Stanford University named John Perry wrote a short, funny essay that became famous among procrastinators around the world. It was called Structured Procrastination. And it began with a confession. Perry admitted that he was a lifelong procrastinator.

But Perry noticed something interesting about himself. Despite procrastinating constantly, he actually got a lot done. He was a productive professor, writing, teaching, serving on committees. How was that possible? His answer was that procrastinators rarely do absolutely nothing. They do things. Just not the thing at the top of their list.

show.cap: A procrastinator who gets things done.

segments.say: Perry noticed that when he was avoiding a big, important task, he would often do other useful things instead. Grading papers, answering letters, tidying his office. Things that were also on his list, but felt easier by comparison. The big task acted as a kind of motivation to do everything else.

show.cap: Busy, just not on the big task

segments.say: So Perry suggested a tongue in cheek strategy. Put a big, important seeming task at the top of your list. One that feels urgent, but perhaps isn't really. Then, as you avoid it, you'll get lots of other valuable things done below it. You use your procrastination, instead of fighting it.

Perry was honest that this involves a little self deception. You have to believe the top task is important and urgent, even when you suspect it isn't entirely. He joked that procrastinators are often excellent at this kind of self deception anyway. So why not put that talent to good use?

The essay became so popular that in two thousand and eleven, Perry received an Ig Nobel Prize for it. The Ig Nobel Prizes are awarded for research that first makes people laugh, and then makes them think. Which is exactly what his essay does. It's funny, but it contains a real insight.

The real insight is that productivity isn't only about forcing ourselves to do the hardest task first. It's also about working with our natural tendencies. If we're going to avoid something anyway, we can at least make sure that the avoidance leads somewhere useful, rather than to an hour of scrolling.

Many people practice a version of this without knowing it. They clean the whole kitchen while avoiding their tax forms. They answer every email while avoiding a difficult phone call. Some call this productive procrastination. It's not perfect. The big task still needs to be done. But it's a lot better than doing nothing.

There's a caution, though. Structured procrastination can become a way of filling your days with easy, small tasks, while the truly important things never get done. Answering emails can feel productive, while the meaningful project sits untouched for months. It's worth checking, now and then, whether your useful avoidance is crowding out what matters most.

I think the deepest gift of Perry's essay is its humor. He looked at his own procrastination with a smile, instead of shame. And that lightness is actually helpful. As we've seen tonight, shame makes procrastination worse. A little humor and self acceptance can make it easier to work with ourselves, rather than against ourselves.

So here's what structured procrastination teaches us. Procrastinators are often busy, just not on the most dreaded task. Avoiding one task can fuel progress on others. It's a useful trick, as long as we check that the important things still get done. And looking at ourselves with humor, instead of shame, makes everything easier.

show.title: Structured procrastination
items: Avoiding one task can fuel others

segments.say: And there's one more powerful way to beat procrastination, perhaps the most powerful of all. Making the task so routine that you never have to decide to do it. Next, let's look at habits, and how they can quietly do the work for us.
